The best alternatives are to find other energy efficient nonpolluting sources or to eliminate the peaks. In view of the alternatives listed in the application for license, the elimination of peak demand is the better alternative.
I understand that study of peak pricing is currently underway in the Duke Power system. The price elasticity of demand will be the determining factor of the study's success. It is possible that revision of the basic rate structure to the point that increased usage increases unit price will enhance the concept of peak pricing.
It should be possible to raise demand during off peak periods in order to "even out" the demand curve by offering power to some large users on an agreed interruptable basis in return for a lower price. The price would be lowered by an amount corresponding to the extra cost of producing power for the peaks. Not all customers could accept an interruptable source, but the amount of power available for production would be increased, in essence, by the amount that would have been wasted by Bad Creek and other pumped storage facilities. This would increase productivity, employment, efficiency of the economy, and Duke Power would not have invested in an energy wasting device. It is within the purposes for which the corporation is organized as set forth in the Articles of Incorporation of Duke Power Company to, if necessary, build and operate such facilities themselves. Of course this would mean an investment, but environmental impact would be minimized, the economy would gain, and energy derived from environmentally degrading sources would be put to use, not to waste.
As a biologist it is enough that Bed Creek threatens a natural area, the environmental integrity of a larger area, a fishery, and the existence of several unique forms. I could oppose most developments on those grounds alone. Peak demand is one thing, need for energy another. The resolution of the two concepts is a moral issue that has yet to be decided. But to allow that environmental degradation and the energy waste inherent in its design for the sake of convenience is intolerable.
I hereby stand with emphatic opposition to the Bad Creek Pumped Storage Project as in the long run it will be detrimental to the best interests of the land, the people, the economy, and therefore, Duke Power Company.
John J. Hagins
(Biologist/ Environmental Laboratories
